usri.title: Student Well-being App
usri.summary: A full research-to-prototype pipeline for a mobile application focused on sleep quality and emotional regulation in university students. Presented at a virtual research conference.

steps.heading: Students struggle to manage sleep and stress, but existing apps don't address the psychological dimension.
steps.body: I started with a structured literature review across sleep science, emotional regulation, and student wellness research. The goal was to validate the problem space before designing anything — confirming that the gap was real, not assumed.

steps.heading: Mapping behavior and psychology before touching Figma.
steps.body: I defined user needs and psychological factors shaping student well-being through behavioral analysis. This produced a research framework that structured every design decision downstream — not a list of features, but a model of why students fail to regulate.

steps.heading: Research artifacts became the interface.
steps.body: Wireframes, a style guide, and an interactive Figma prototype were built directly from research findings. No arbitrary decisions — each component traces back to a validated user need or behavioral insight.

steps.heading: Think-aloud sessions + pre/post surveys to measure real shift in perception.
steps.body: I designed and facilitated usability sessions, collecting both qualitative pain points and quantitative perception data. Findings were synthesized via affinity diagrams and journey maps to surface what to change and why.

steps.heading: Final prototype presented at a virtual research conference.
steps.body: The process produced a refined, tested prototype that demonstrated measurable improvement in usability perception. The full research-to-presentation cycle was completed within a single summer internship.

nano.title: Nanobanana Feature Enhancement
nano.summary: Identified that creative terminology was locking beginner users out of a photo tool. Redesigned the prompting experience entirely — replacing text with visual selectors.

steps.heading: Beginners couldn't get started because the tool spoke in expert language.
steps.body: Through informal research in online communities, I confirmed that the main barrier wasn't capability — it was vocabulary. Users didn't know what "Rembrandt lighting" or "Dutch angle" meant, so they couldn't use the tool at all.

steps.heading: The gap was in the language layer, not the feature itself.
steps.body: The existing text-based prompt input assumed prior knowledge. The fix wasn't a glossary — it was removing the assumption entirely. If users could see options rather than name them, the vocabulary barrier disappears.

steps.heading: Visual selectors for angle, lighting, and composition — no terminology required.
steps.body: I designed a feature that replaces text prompts with visual selection grids. Users choose what they want by looking, not describing. Each selection is a visual sample, not a label.

steps.heading: Reduced cognitive load, increased exploration, better onboarding.
steps.body: The redesign made the tool approachable without simplifying its power. Non-experts could now explore options they previously didn't know existed. Engagement improved because understanding improved.

word.title: Wordtropolis
word.summary: A gamified spelling learning platform designed for young students. Identified the core failures of traditional spelling tools and rebuilt the experience around how children actually learn.

steps.heading: Spelling tools are boring by design — and that's a design failure.
steps.body: Existing tools suffered from low engagement, static interaction, and unclear feedback. Children were learning despite the interface, not because of it. The root issue: these tools were built around content delivery, not the psychology of how kids actually retain and stay motivated.

steps.heading: How do children learn? Through play, feedback, and visible progress.
steps.body: I grounded the redesign in learning science: intrinsic motivation, spaced repetition, and multi-sensory reinforcement. The system needed to feel like a game — where the learning is the mechanic, not a layer on top of it.

steps.heading: Missions → boss battle progression to sustain motivation over time.
steps.body: I designed a narrative-driven progression system with clear milestones, visual feedback, and a boss battle as the culminating challenge. The arc gave children a reason to return — and a sense of accomplishment when they did.

steps.heading: Figma prototype → implemented in Java Swing with adaptive difficulty.
steps.body: The full interactive prototype was built and implemented. Adaptive learning adjusted difficulty based on performance. Multi-sensory feedback (visual, auditory cues) reinforced correct responses and kept the experience legible for young users.

steps.heading: An engaging system that aligns interface design with how children actually learn.
steps.body: Wordtropolis demonstrated that the gap between educational software and effective learning is a design problem — not a content problem. A well-designed interaction loop can make practice feel like play.
